utterance: Grace, thank you for coming in. Today I want to go through the pension form line by line, in plain language, and decide nothing. Is that all right?
Yes please. I brought the form. I don't understand half of it.
This line says survivor benefit: sixty percent of Samuel's monthly pension, paid to you for life.
For life. And it doesn't go down?
Not unless the plan itself changes, which would be unusual. The form doesn't mention increases, so I'd plan on it staying level. I'll ask the plan administrator to confirm that.
Level. So prices go up and it stays the same.
Yes. That's partly why I raised the annuity. Someone might offer to cover that. I'd like you to understand the trade before choosing.
The man says guaranteed. Guaranteed is a nice word.
It is. It's only as good as the company and the contract, and it costs you access to the money.
And this part, the lump sum?
The form offers a lump sum instead of the monthly payments. I haven't evaluated it and I'm not recommending it. I'll compare the two and bring you the numbers.
I think I'd rather have the monthly money. I like knowing it comes. But please don't write that down as final.
Understood. I'll note a preference for monthly income, not a decision, until my comparison is done.
And the annuity. I'm feeling like no. But I don't know.
You don't have to know today. Let's set a decision call for the twenty-sixth.
The twenty-sixth. Good. Thank you for not rushing me.
Lucas, you've had the comparison since Friday. Where are you?
I read it twice. Half is where I keep landing. But I haven't talked to my accountant about the tax.

Let me tell you what I think, including where I disagree with you. Selling nothing keeps all the upside, but you have tax payments coming, a reserve to build, and a single-company stake. I'd sell something. I lean toward half.
You always say sell something.
Because it's true. But my recommendation isn't your decision.
What would selling all do?
It cleans up the risk, but you give up the company's upside and probably pay more tax this year. I wouldn't recommend all.
Okay. And if I sell half I still have a stake.
A large one.
Give me until next week. When's the paperwork due?
The offer letter says April 17.
So decide by the 14th, sign by the 17th.
That works. Ask your accountant about the tax before then.
Yeah, yeah.
Hi Sofia, how is Lucia?
Amazing and exhausting. She's nearly sleeping five hours in a row, which feels like a miracle.
That's wonderful. Today I'd like to talk about going back to work. When we last spoke you said your manager had floated a four-day week for when you return from leave.
He hinted at it, in passing, in a one-to-one. He said "we could look at four days when you're back." Nothing formal.
What would that do to your income?
About twenty percent less salary. I don't want to do the maths.
I can do it for you. A fifth off salary is a big hole next to childcare.
Right. So I don't want to ask for it. I might. Part of me wants Fridays with Lucia.
Both of those are valid. I'll model it as a scenario so you can see it, and I'll treat it as a possibility only.
Yes. Please don't write "Sofia is going to four days."
I'll record it as: your manager hinted, you haven't asked, and you're undecided.
Perfect.
One practical thing. Have you got a childcare place yet?
We have one lined up for when I'm back. I'll send you the fees when I have them.
Please do. That's the number I need most.
Morning, Kenji. I've updated the scenarios since our April 22 call to include the retention bonus. Can I walk you through them, and then ask what you and Mariko have worked out?
Please. I read your summary, but I'd like to hear it. Is the bonus counted at the full hundred and fifty thousand?

Pre-tax, yes, but only in the 63 scenario, paid in installments for as long as you stay. I haven't counted it at 60, because on the terms as I read them you'd forfeit it. I still haven't seen the retention agreement itself, so treat those terms as provisional.
I have the agreement. I'll upload it to the portal today.
Thank you. With the bonus, 63 funds the fifteen thousand a month target with a reasonable margin. 65 has a comfortable margin, as before. My suggestion is that 63 is the age to test, rather than 60.
That's fair. 60 is off the table in my head unless Northgate is sold and the role disappears. But I'm not ready to say 63 is the answer.
Understood. So what I'll hold today is this: 63 is under serious consideration, and the formal planning date is still 65.
Yes. Mariko and I talked on Sunday. She wants me out before 65, but she's nervous about the healthcare gap. She'd be happier with 63 than 65.
What worries her most about healthcare?
The two thousand eight hundred a month you estimated for private cover until Medicare. She wants to see that number in the plan, not just in my head.
It's in the 63 scenario for the full two years. I can show it as its own line so she can see it.
Please do. My brother also called. He thinks I'm crazy to stay on for a bonus at Northgate.
What do you think?
I think the bonus is real money and I'd be here until 63 anyway. I'm not letting him decide this.
Then here is what I'd suggest. You and Mariko take a few days. If you reach a decision, tell me on our May 1 call and I'll change the planning date then, not before.
Agreed. I'll tell you on Friday. Nothing changes in the file until I say so.
Rebecca, thanks for making time. One topic today: Ethan's college. On February 19 you said there's about eighty-five thousand in the account David started. Is that still right?
As of the April statement, yes. About eighty-five. Ethan applies this autumn.
Do you have a sense of what the schools on his list cost?
A mix of private and state. I don't want him choosing a school on price.

Understood, and I'll plan for that. Say private at about eighty thousand a year all-in. Four years is three hundred twenty thousand. The account covers roughly a quarter of it. The rest comes from income and, later, from the sale proceeds.
After the sale closes. Not before. Don't plan Ethan's college on money that isn't in my account yet.
Fair. I'll show two versions: one funded from income only, and one that includes the proceeds.
Do that.
Separately, a suggestion: a 529 plan could hold part of what you set aside. With a start date this close, the tax benefit is smaller, so I wouldn't rush it.
What's the downside?
Less flexibility if he gets scholarships or goes a different route, though there are exceptions.
I'm not sure I want to open one. Ask me again once I know where he's applying.
Then it stays open. I'll hold the 529 as a suggestion and I won't set anything up.
Right. David thinks state schools are fine. I'm the one pushing private. We'll sort that out at home.
Understood. I'll model both so you have the numbers when you do.
Good. My mother's reserve next time. I want to keep this short today.
You raised Lisbon on the 7th and I wrote it down as a possibility. Has anything changed?
Camille asked HR about working remotely. They said they'd get back to her.
And Moreau Labs?
I could run it from anywhere. But my two biggest customers like having me in the room.
Then there are two conditions: her employer saying yes, and the company not needing you in the room. Before anything else, a cross-border tax specialist would be worth a conversation.
I'm not paying a specialist for a maybe.
Fair. Then it stays a maybe and I won't plan around it.
Yes. If HR says yes, I'll tell you and we'll look at it properly.
I'll keep it recorded as a possibility with those two conditions.
Right. Send me a short note so I remember what I said.
I'll do that.
Peg, good morning. Take your time. Today I thought we'd go through the contract together and write down the questions for the attorney.
Yes, dear. I wrote some things on the back of an envelope.
Lovely. First, the entrance fee: three hundred eighty thousand dollars. The contract says eighty percent comes back to the estate.
So twenty percent is gone.
Yes. That's roughly seventy-six thousand that wouldn't come back.
That's a lot of money for a room.
It also buys the right to nursing care later. The question is whether you'd use it.
Frank wants to stay home. But he can't tell me what he'll want when he's worse.
That's the honest uncertainty. Second, the monthly fee can rise.
By how much?
That's a question for the attorney: whether there's a cap.
I'll ask. What else?
Whether a change in Frank's care needs would trigger a move to the nursing wing, and who decides.
I'll write that down.
I'm not recommending yes or no. The decision stays yours.
I know, dear. Frank and I will decide. I don't want to be rushed.
Good morning, Kenji. I've read the election form. Shall I go through my comments before you submit it?
Yes. I've decided on five installments starting at 63, so I mostly want a second pair of eyes.

Two comments. The form asks for a beneficiary if you die before the installments finish, and it's blank. And the start-date field says age 63, but the plan defines it as the first January after your 63rd birthday. Check that matches what Hannah assumed in her estimate.
I don't know what she assumed. I'll ask her.
Please ask her to confirm it in writing so it's on file. On the beneficiary, who do you want?
Mariko first, then Yuki and Ren equally. I'd like to confirm that against the estate documents, though.
That makes sense, and I'm collecting your wills and designations anyway. Do you want Mariko on the form now, with the contingent names to follow?
Yes. Mariko as primary now. Contingent names after the documents review.
For the record, neither payout option was my recommendation. I said I wouldn't choose until we saw Hannah's numbers. Five installments is your decision, and I think it's a reasoned one.
Good. The administrator's deadline is June 26. I'd like to submit by the 19th.
That works. Send me the signed copy afterwards so it's on file.
Will do.
Separately, the fourteen thousand for Ren's semester is still earmarked. Have you heard about his acceptance?
Nothing yet. They said end of June.
Then I'll leave the earmark as it is and we'll check at the half-year review.
Good.
Sofia, thanks for sending the childcare fees on Friday. I've put them in the budget draft. Before our Wednesday call, I'd like to show you how the gap looks.
Okay. I'm scared of this slide.
The gap is manageable. There are three ways to cover it: trim your brokerage contributions, use part of the house fund, or reduce your 401(k) contributions. I'd rule out touching the 401(k) match.
Agreed. The match stays.
Between the other two, my instinct is that the house fund is the cleaner cushion for a short period, because it's sitting in cash.
Hmm. I guess? Let me see the numbers on Wednesday.
Of course. I'm suggesting, not deciding.
Okay. Don't put that in as done.
I won't. I'll show it as one option among three.
Thank you. Mateo says he's still deciding about that interview, by the way. Nothing yet.
Understood. I won't plan around it until there's an actual offer.

I don't want her to feel I don't trust her.

Up to $15,000, only as a gift, from the insurance payout. You haven't set a date.
Correct. Not yet.
